subtype: Approach: practising old test papers under time [Action]
passage: I'm Vikram, and last Sunday I sat down at our dining table and solved last year's maths paper. My sister Vinita put the clock in front of me and sat with her chin on her hand. "Start!" I got through the first questions quickly. Then question seven took me a long time. "Bhaiya, fifteen minutes on that one," Vinita said. I checked my answers with the answer sheet afterwards. I got most of the paper right, but I ran out of time at the end, and the last three questions were empty. I decided to skip any hard question, mark it, and come back to it if there was time left.

qa.q: Who put the clock in front of Vikram?
qa.a: His sister Vinita put the clock in front of him.

qa.q: What did Vikram feel when he saw the last three questions were empty?
qa.a: He felt disappointed and a bit annoyed with himself, since the time had gone on one hard question.

qa.q: What else could Vikram do to improve his timing, and why?
qa.a: He could decide how many minutes each question deserves before he begins. Then he will know when to move on.

qa.q: How does Vinita see Vikram's practice paper?
qa.a: Vinita sees a brother who lost time on one question, and she called out the minutes. She helped him notice it without giving answers.

grounding: A boy solves last year's maths paper with a clock, checks his answers and learns he spends too long on one question, so he decides to skip and return.

subtype: Approach: practising old test papers under time [Action]
passage: Note for Vijay's tuition sir, Sunday. As you suggested, Vijay did the maths paper from last year on the dining table this afternoon, with the kitchen clock in front of him and one hour allowed. I watched from the stove. He spent almost twenty minutes on question 6, the one about the train, rubbing out again and again. When time was up he had not reached questions 9 and 10. We checked together: most of what he did was right. He said, without any prompting, "Next time I'll mark the hard one, skip it and come back." We'll try another paper on Wednesday. Aparna

qa.q: How long did Vijay spend on question 6?
How did Vijay seem to feel after checking the paper?
qa.a: He seemed a little frustrated at running out of time but encouraged that most of his answers were right, so he wanted to fix the timing.

qa.q: What else could Vijay try in Wednesday's paper?
qa.a: Glance at the clock after every few questions and set a rough limit per question; the timed practice is what showed his problem.

qa.q: How does Aparna see the practice session?
qa.a: Aparna is pleased that Vijay spotted the timing problem himself, without prompting, and plans another paper.

grounding: Shows a boy doing last year's maths paper against a clock, checking it, and deciding to skip a slow question and return to it.

subtype: Approach: practising old test papers under time [Action]
passage:
Saturday
Did the maths paper from last year today, at our dining table, with Mummy's alarm clock set for ninety minutes, just like the real exam. Sudha didi was the invigilator (she took it very seriously). I got stuck on the geometry question with the circle and kept trying for ages. When the alarm rang I still had three questions left, and two of them were easy! I checked my answers with the key at the back: 58 out of 80. Most marks lost were on the three I never reached. Sudha didi said, 'Deepak bhai, you let one question eat your time.' She's right. Next paper: if a question takes too long, I circle it, skip it and come back.

qa.q: What did Deepak score on the practice paper?
How did Deepak feel when he saw two of the unreached questions were easy?
qa.a: Deepak felt frustrated, since easy marks were lost only because one hard question ate the time.

qa.q: Is Deepak's new rule a good one, and what could make it stronger?
qa.a: Yes; he could also set a rough time limit per question, so he knows when 'too long' has arrived.

qa.q: How does Sudha see her role and Deepak's mistake?
qa.a: Sudha takes being invigilator seriously and says plainly that one question ate his time, so she seems keen to help him improve.

grounding: Illustrates a boy timing himself on last year's maths paper, checking it, and deciding to skip a slow question and come back later.
